clue.text: Some howlers from heartless member of Bloomsbury Set / Group

indicators.note: heartless asks for the central letter of the writer's surname to be removed

parts.note: Virginia Woolf was a leading member of the Bloomsbury Set of writers and artists
a group or band of animals is a pack

explanation.surface: Someone gathers the gaffes made by a cold-hearted Bloomsbury writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' drops the middle O of WOOLF, leaving WOLF. 'Howlers' looks like blunders, but here it means animals that howl.
explanation.definitionFit: Wolves howl, so a band of them hunting together is some howlers.

clue.text: Where to find Talbothays Dairy and join up with it

indicators.note: in a down entry up means read from the bottom, so the stitching word is reversed

parts.note: to sew is to join with stitches
it is a slang term for sex appeal

explanation.surface: A dairy farmer is told where the farm is and invited to link up with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns SEW into WES. Talbothays Dairy is where Tess works in Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hardy set his novels in a fictional south-western English region based on Dorset and its neighbours.

clue.text: "Such hath it been — shall be — beneath the sun / The many still must — for the one" (The Corsair, Byron)

definitions.text: "Such hath it been — shall be — beneath the sun / The many still must — for the one" (The Corsair, Byron)

parts.words: "Such hath it been — shall be — beneath the sun / The many still must — for the one" (The Corsair, Byron)
parts.note: a quotation from Byron with one word missing: the verb meaning toil, which the many must do for the benefit of one ruler

explanation.definitionFit: In The Corsair Byron says the many must toil for the one, so the missing word is a verb of hard work.

clue.text: King novel and short story by Vidal carried by Venetian executive

indicators.note: carried by means held inside, so the explorer's name goes round the other pieces

parts.note: Marco Polo, the traveller to China, was a Venetian
It is a horror novel by Stephen King

indicators.note: short means missing its last letter

parts.note: Burr is a historical novel by Gore Vidal about Aaron Burr

explanation.surface: Novels by Stephen King and Gore Vidal are carried by a Venetian business chief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims BURR to BUR. 'Venetian executive' suggests the Doge, but the Venetian is Marco Polo and 'executive' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Politburo was the chief policy-making committee of a Communist party, its executive body.

clue.text: Maurice's friend supporting Dracula-like northern area?

indicators.note: in a down entry supporting means placed underneath, so the friend comes second

parts.note: Dracula was a count, so like a count is jokingly county
Clive Durham is Maurice's friend and lover in E. M. Forster's novel Maurice

explanation.surface: Maurice's friend props up a region that looks like Dracula's.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun of county as count-like. County Durham is a county in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: County Durham is an administrative region of north-east England.

clue.text: Villainous manservant in strange book

parts.note: strange means odd
Job is a book of the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A wicked servant appears in a peculiar novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Oddjob is Auric Goldfinger's murderous Korean henchman and servant in Ian Fleming's Goldfinger.

clue.text: Perhaps reading poem set in far reaches of Dorset coast

indicators.note: set in means placed inside, so the letters go between the county's ends
the far reaches are the extremities, so the first and last letters of the county

parts.note: reading is one of the three Rs, so R
If is Rudyard Kipling's famous poem

explanation.surface: A poem about reading is set on the far edges of the Dorset shoreline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dorset coast' looks like one place, but 'coast' is the verb being defined; 'set in' places the reading letter and Kipling's poem between the county's outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To coast is to move along without effort, as a boat or idler might drift.

clue.text: AI may, to begin with, fix VS Reid?

indicators.note: to begin with puts the predicament word at the front of the assembly

parts.note: a fix is a jam, a tight spot
may, meaning be able to, can stand for can

explanation.surface: Asks whether artificial intelligence could repair a writer's mistakes at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: V. S. Reid was a Jamaican novelist, author of New Day; the question mark marks him as an example. 'AI' looks like artificial intelligence but is just its two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Victor Stafford Reid was born in Kingston, so he is an example of an islander from the Caribbean.

clue.text: Males uncovered Twilight author's target

parts.note: bulls are male cattle

indicators.note: uncovered means stripped of its outer layer, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: Stephenie Meyer wrote the Twilight vampire novels

explanation.surface: Men exposed as the Twilight author's quarry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncovered' strips MEYER to EYE.
explanation.definitionFit: The bullseye is the centre of a dartboard or archery target, so it stands for the target itself.

clue.text: Garcia Marquez's agreed with book by priest and American composer

parts.note: the Colombian novelist wrote in Spanish, where yes is si
Eli is the priest of Shiloh in the Book of Samuel
US is short for American, as in US citizen

explanation.surface: The Colombian novelist backs a book written by a cleric and an American musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American composer' reads as one phrase, but the composer is Finnish; American only gives US.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Sibelius was the Finnish symphonist who wrote Finlandia.

clue.text: Drab manuscript in set that's rejected

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the whole assembly is read backwards
in places the abbreviation inside the word for set

parts.note: set, as of a table, means laid

explanation.surface: A dull document sits in a collection that has been turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' builds LAMSID, and 'that's rejected' turns that whole run round. 'Drab' could be a noun for a slattern, but here it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Drab and dismal both describe something cheerless and dreary.

clue.text: Briefly write new Grahame novel, like The Wind in the Willows?

definitions.text: like The Wind in the Willows?

indicators.note: novel means new and different, so these letters are rearranged
briefly means cut short, so the last letter of the verb goes

parts.note: write is taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to write a new Kenneth Grahame novel in the spirit of his riverbank classic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' leaves WRIT; 'novel', which looks like a noun, shuffles WRIT, N and GRAHAME. Kenneth Grahame wrote The Wind in the Willows.
explanation.definitionFit: Grahame's riverbank tale of Mole, Ratty and Toad is famously cosy and uplifting.

clue.text: Break out rejected introduction to The Innocent

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the synonym for innocent is read backwards

parts.note: innocent means pure

indicators.note: an introduction is the opening, so only the first letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: An escape is refused at the opening of a story called The Innocent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns PURE into ERUP. The capitalised 'The Innocent' looks like a title (Ian McEwan wrote one), but only its letters are used.
explanation.definitionFit: To erupt is to burst forth suddenly, as a volcano or a riot does.

clue.text: Cast at odds with their stagecraft

indicators.note: being at odds means out of harmony, so the letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: A cast disagrees with the way their play is staged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at odds with' shuffles CAST and THEIR together. 'Cast' looks like the actors, but it is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatrics means the craft of staging plays, the business of the theatre.

clue.text: Male anger — not female — about illness almost overcoming queen in Christie novel

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the shortened rage goes round the rest
not female asks for the letter F, the abbreviation for female, to be taken away

parts.note: anger means fury

indicators.note: overcoming means lying over, so the sickness takes the royal letters inside it
almost means one letter short of complete

parts.note: illness means disease
ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for the queen

explanation.surface: A man's rage over a sickness that nearly beats a queen in a whodunnit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not female' leaves URY; 'almost' and 'overcoming' make DERISEAS, the queen inside the shortened sickness; 'about' wraps URY round that. The dashes only fence off the deletion.
explanation.definitionFit: This 1939 Agatha Christie mystery is set in an English village where several deaths are disguised as accidents.

clue.text: Kate does without love, yet ultimately is most canny

parts.note: Kate is the title character of Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the zero letter is removed

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, so O

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Kate manages without love, and in the end she proves the cleverest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' takes O from DOES to leave DES; 'ultimately' gives the T of 'yet'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrewd means astute and sharp, and canny means the same, so most canny is shrewdest.

clue.text: Patron's translation of Roget's, say, turned up

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, so the definition is a patron, here a patron saint

indicators.note: a translation renders words in a new form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the name is taken with its possessive S as fodder

indicators.note: in a down entry turned up means read from the bottom, so the abbreviation is reversed

parts.note: say means for example, abbreviated EG

explanation.surface: A patron's translation of a thesaurus has appeared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translation of' rearranges ROGETS into STGEOR and 'turned up' makes EG into GE. The 's of 'Patron's' means is.
explanation.definitionFit: The dragon-slaying saint is the patron saint of England.

clue.text: Lawful to probe eccentric rival to Abbess of Crewe

indicators.note: to probe means to go inside, so the legal word goes into the odd one

parts.note: fey means whimsical, eccentric
licit means lawful

explanation.surface: A lawful inquiry into an odd competitor of the Abbess of Crewe.
explanation.walkthrough: The Abbess of Crewe is Muriel Spark's novella about a rigged convent election.
explanation.definitionFit: Sister Felicity is Alexandra's opponent in the election for abbess in Muriel Spark's The Abbess of Crewe.

clue.text: Brothers wore out story of The Clocks

indicators.note: worn out suggests something broken down, so these letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: Siblings grew tired of an Agatha Christie mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges BROTHERS and WORE together. 'The Clocks' looks like Christie's novel, but here it is the family name of the tiny people in Mary Norton's books.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Norton's children's book follows Pod, Homily and Arrietty Clock, tiny people living under the floor.

clue.text: Star is avoiding MacLean

indicators.note: avoiding means keeping clear of, so the two letters are left out

parts.note: Alistair MacLean was the Scottish thriller writer of The Guns of Navarone

explanation.surface: A celebrity is giving a thriller writer a wide berth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' looks like a celebrity, but it is a star in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Altair is the brightest star in the constellation Aquila.

clue.text: Child bitten by snake in bed?

indicators.note: bitten by means held in the jaws of, so the author's name goes inside the snake

parts.note: an asp is a venomous snake
Lee Child is the author of the Jack Reacher thrillers

explanation.surface: A youngster is bitten by a serpent in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Child' looks like a youngster; it is the thriller writer Lee Child. The question mark flags that being in bed need not mean sleeping.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in bed usually means to be sleeping, dead to the world.

clue.text: Heath, not quite prime minister, changed name

indicators.note: not quite asks for the plant word without its final letter

parts.note: erica is the botanical name for heath, the heather plant
Tony Blair was the UK prime minister from 1997 to 2007

explanation.surface: A former prime minister, Heath, falls a little short and is renamed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heath' looks like Edward Heath, another prime minister; it is the plant. 'not quite' drops the last letter of ERICA.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric Blair took the pen name George Orwell, so his birth name was changed.

clue.text: Shrub seen at first in Brideshead Revisited, intriguing Edward Ryder

indicators.note: at first in asks for the opening letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: A bush appears early in Waugh's Brideshead Revisited, intriguing its narrator.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Ryder is the narrator of Evelyn Waugh's Brideshead Revisited; 'Edward' is only a letter here.
explanation.definitionFit: A brier is a thorny bush such as the wild rose.

clue.text: Sci-fi pioneer's English city

definitions.meaning: H. G. ..., author of The Time Machine, was an early writer of science fiction
... in Somerset is England's smallest city, with a cathedral

explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the Time Machine author is also a Somerset cathedral city's name.

clue.text: Detective Agatha's mentioning briefly

definitions.note: the clue refers to the surname belonging to the sleuth, so the possessive names it

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the final letter goes

parts.note: mentioning a topic is raising it

explanation.surface: The detective Agatha is being spoken of in passing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Agatha' sends you to Christie, whose name runs through this puzzle; the sleuth here is M. C. Beaton's.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Raisin is the amateur sleuth of M. C. Beaton's Cotswolds novels.

clue.text: Scholarly American volume put away

parts.note: liter is the American spelling of litre, a measure of volume
to put away food is to eat it, so ate

explanation.surface: An academic American book gets shelved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'volume' looks like a book; it is a measure of capacity.
explanation.definitionFit: Literate can mean well read and educated as well as able to read.

clue.text: Gloomy sort of early English history

parts.note: EE is the abbreviation for Early English, the style of Gothic architecture
yore means times long past, history

explanation.surface: A depressing variety of the early history of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' looks like it qualifies 'early English history', but 'sort' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The melancholy donkey in A. A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh books is the classic gloomy character.

clue.text: Soldier breaking at support for brainwashing literature?

indicators.note: breaking means splitting open, so the soldier goes inside the little word

parts.note: GI is an American soldier
a prop is a support

explanation.surface: A soldier breaks in to support the brainwashing of readers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' splits the little word open around the soldier. The question mark flags that propaganda leaflets and plays are only loosely literature.
explanation.definitionFit: Agitprop is political propaganda, especially in art and writing, meant to indoctrinate.
